name: Aurelia 'Madame Aurelie' Tierney
languages: Irish (her grandmother's, which she uses on stage as the language of the spirits)
equipment: A plum silk dress, a theatrical hat with a black veil, and good gloves; her one respectable outfit
A black silk reticule, and in it the pocket revolver
Pocket revolver (.32), bought after a client's husband followed her home in 1890
Kitchen knife, small and very sharp, in the reticule, for cutting a cord at a séance, or anything else
A séance kit in a carpetbag: two school slates and chalk, a folding tin trumpet, a tambourine, a pot of luminous paint, black gauze, and a shoe with a loose heel for rapping
A deck of cards for cold readings, and a flask of gin
A cabinet photograph of her late husband, Danny, a stagehand, in his Sunday suit
Three of her printed cards: MADAME AURELIE. SITTINGS. COMMUNICATIONS. ATLANTIC AVENUE, BROOKLYN
features: The Thin Place (Sensitive: knows when a presence is within 60 ft, though not where; feels cold spots and wrongness first; the GM tells you the strongest emotion soaked into each room you enter. Once per scene, open yourself to the place and receive one true impression of a presence, an event or what the thing wants, at the cost of 1 Dread with no save. Never control, never magic)
Read the Room (Sensitive: advantage on Insight to tell what a person feels; knows without a check when someone you speak with is frightened, grieving or hiding something, though not what)

Closer to the Edge (Sensitive, 2nd level: Dread from The Thin Place can't take you past 5; at Dread 3 or higher The Thin Place gives two impressions, and you can place a presence within 60 ft to within 10 ft)

Been Here Before (Survivor origin: advantage on initiative; when a fight or fright begins you know the nearest way out; once per long rest reroll a failed saving throw, including a fear check; the first time each scenario you meet a horror like the one you survived, the GM tells you one way it is the same)

The Séance Trade (Medium background: spiritualist circles, performers and grieving families welcome her; she can arrange a séance anywhere with a day's notice; she spots another performer's tricks without a check, and the GM tells her when something in a room is not a trick. The background grants nothing supernatural)

personality.traits: On stage I am Madame Aurelie, low-voiced, mysterious, faintly French. Off it I am Aurelia Tierney of Atlantic Avenue, and I talk like a Brooklyn dresser, which is what I was. I can read a room in a second and I can never stop doing it.
personality.ideals: People come to me grieving, and I send them home lighter. Whether anybody is really talking to them is between them and God. I give good value.
personality.bonds: Danny, dead four years. The memory of the night of the theatre fire, and everyone I could not get out. Old Mr. Abraham, who came to my sittings in July and cried, and turned out to be Jasper Greywick, and left me a thousand dollars.
personality.flaws: I am a fraud, mostly, and I have got used to it. I bribed this house's coachman five dollars to find out who Mr. Abraham was. And sometimes it is not a trick, and I am more afraid of that than anything.

appearance: A striking woman of thirty-six with a mass of dark red hair, a pale freckled face she powders very white for the stage, large green eyes that never stop moving, a small scar along her left jaw, and a beautiful low voice she can drop into a Brooklyn rasp in an instant. Too much jet jewellery for a mourning house.
backstory: Aurelia Tierney was born in Brooklyn in 1857 to an Irish longshoreman and a mother who read tea leaves for the neighbours. At nineteen she was a dresser at the Brooklyn Theatre on the night of the fire in December 1876, and got eleven people out through a scene dock door before the roof came in, and has never since been able to sleep in a room without knowing where the door is. She married Danny Tierney, a stagehand, in 1880; he died of pneumonia in 1889. She learned the séance trade from a medium she dressed for, and for ten years has given sittings in a parlour on Atlantic Avenue, mostly technique: cold reading, a loose heel, a trumpet, a slate with a message already on its underside. Mostly. In July 1893 a sad old gentleman calling himself Mr. Abraham came to four sittings and asked each time for a lady who had died on the river. Aurelia bribed his coachman, who had brought him down from the Hudson, and learned his name; she had a fine message ready for the fourth sitting. She never delivered it. Instead, with the room gone cold and the candle lying flat, she heard herself say, in a voice that was not hers, 'She wants her name,' and Jasper Greywick wept and paid her a hundred dollars and never came back. The will leaves her $1,000, 'who heard her'. Leonora Greywick has asked her to hold a sitting on Tuesday night. (Hooks: the séance in gw-scenario-002; The Thin Place in the north wing; the coachman Pruyn Hasselt knows what she paid him; she is the first person to hear the Juffrouw speak through her.)
